principle: Themes borrow a genre's grammar: light, palette mood, type feel, camera language, edit rhythm and sound texture. They borrow nothing a studio owns. A style can't be owned, but logos, characters and specific creative expression can.
borrow: Open-license faces with the right temperament.
Push-ins, crawls, tracking shots, crash zooms.
On the beat, on twos, held pauses.
Hum, hiss, tape, room tone. Never a melody.
never_ship: Franchise names, logos, wordmarks or title-card lockups, including look-alike recreations.
Characters, creatures, likenesses, costumes, or silhouettes that read as a specific character.
Named places, organizations, ships, products or invented terms from the work.
Scores, sound-alikes of a theme melody, or signature sound effects.
Stills, frames, posters, or traced compositions of specific shots.
The franchise's own typefaces. Use the open-license fonts on each card and record them in the manifest.
naming: Public pages, meta tags, alt text, repositories and client deliverables use the codename only ("TX-07 NIGHT DRIVE"), never a franchise name with "-style" after it. Internal briefs may name the inspiration. Nothing may imply endorsement or affiliation.
swap_test: Picture the theme swapped for its nearest genre neighbor. Any element that only makes sense as one franchise's property gets cut or redesigned. Log homage-check: PASS or FAIL at the T stage.
commentary: A story that is about a film or franchise (a fan community, a review, a cultural analysis) may name it in copy as factual reference. It still uses no logos or studio assets, and carries the property's disclaimer where one exists. If a client asks for a licensed look, escalate to Barry.
public_edition: This repository is the public edition of the codex. Inspiration names and the shipped-property ledger stay in BHIL's internal brief. The validator enforces this with a salted, hashed deny list, so the list itself never ships.
